sentences.text: Toby did not tell his mother about the manuscript.
He did not know why he did not tell her.
Maybe because she was sad about closing the store and he did not want to make it worse.
Maybe because he wanted to read it first, alone, before anyone else did.
He hid the manuscript in his school backpack.
He took it home.
He read it in his room, under his desk lamp, after his parents had gone to bed.
The book was about a boy named Toby.
It was about a boy who was starting sixth grade at a school on the north side of Chicago.
It was about a boy who had a best friend named Marcus and a dog named Waffle and a favorite hot chocolate from the coffee shop across from his apartment.
It was about a boy who was being pushed around at school by another boy named Ryan Callahan.
Real Toby, sitting under his desk lamp, felt something cold slide down his back.
Real Toby went to school with a real boy named Ryan Callahan.
And Ryan Callahan had, twice a week for the last month, taken things out of Toby's locker and hidden them, and shoved Toby in the hall, and called Toby names.
Real Toby had not told anybody about it.
The book kept going.
It described what real Toby had eaten for breakfast this morning.
It described a conversation real Toby had with his mother last week about whether he was okay, and how real Toby had said "I'm fine" even though he wasn't.
How did his grandmother know?
She could not have known.
She had written this in 1998.
She had been forty-six years old.
She had not even met Toby's mother yet.
Toby's father was a stranger to her.
There was no Waffle in 1998.
But there she was, on page 87, describing Waffle.
Down to the small brown spot on Waffle's left ear.
By Chapter 11, Toby in the book had had enough.
He was sitting at the kitchen table with his father, and he was about to say something.
Real Toby held his breath.
"Dad," said Toby in the book.
"I need to talk to you about something.
There's a kid at school —"
The chapter ended there.
Real Toby turned the page.
The next page said, at the top: CHAPTER 12.
The rest of the page was blank.
So was the next page.
And the next.
The manuscript ended.
The story stopped.
There was a post-it note on the blank page.
Grandma Ada's handwriting, faded but clear.
It said: FINISH THIS WHEN YOU KNOW HOW.
